title: A new king (Exodus 1:8–14)
hook: a Pharaoh who didn't know Joseph fears the Hebrews and enslaves them

segments.voice: Yesterday, Genesis close: a garden at the start, a coffin in Egypt at the end. Your line was broken people, kept promises. Which promise did you keep? Day three hundred seventy-seven.

A new book. Jews call it Shemot, names, after its opening words: these are the names of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt. Christians call it Exodus, the Greek word for the way out. It starts where Genesis left off. Joseph dies. His brothers die. That whole generation dies. And their children are fruitful, the text says, and multiply, until the land is filled with them. For a while, things are fine. A family that came down for bread has become a people. And then comes one sentence, and the whole story turns on it.
screen: `SHEMOT: NAMES.` → `EXODUS: THE WAY OUT.` → `A FAMILY BECOMES A PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph." A generation passes, and someone forgot. Forgot the man who saved Egypt from famine. Forgot why these people were here at all. And forgetting makes room for fear. The new king says to his people: look, these Israelites are more and mightier than we are. Let's deal wisely with them, or if a war comes, they'll join our enemies. It's an old move. Take neighbors, call them a threat, and act before they can do anything. So the Egyptians set taskmasters over them to wear them down with heavy labor. They build store cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses. "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew." The plan backfires, so the oppression tightens. The text says the Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in mortar and brick and all kinds of work in the field. Bitter is a word that will come back. Exodus will later tell Israel to eat the Passover with bitter herbs, and Jews still eat them at the Seder. Notice also what Exodus doesn't say. It never names this Pharaoh. Historians have proposed different kings, and some doubt we can place the story in Egyptian records at all. The book seems less interested in which king than in what kind. Before anyone is rescued, the book shows how it went wrong. Exodus is a story of God hearing people who cry out, and it starts with a ruler who didn't remember.
screen: `A NEW KING, WHICH KNEW NOT JOSEPH.` · `FEAR: THEY ARE MORE THAN WE.` · `THE MORE THEY AFFLICTED THEM.` · `LIVES MADE BITTER.` · then, large: `WHICH KNEW NOT JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold people in forced labor today. Settle, and breathe. Think about the things around you: your clothes, your phone, the food in your kitchen. Somewhere in the chains that made them, there may be people working who are not free to leave. You don't know their names. Picture them anyway, tired hands, bricks of their own. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, hold them in mind, and let yourself remember them. The bell holds the time.
A new king. The Pharaoh who knew not Joseph, who feared the Israelites and made their lives bitter with forced labor.
Your line: someone forgot. Today, find out one thing about where something you use every day was made, and who made it. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Christians read Exodus as the story of God hearing the cry of the oppressed (Exodus 2:23–25; 3:7), and some churches draw on its opening chapters when they pray about forced labor and trafficking today.

fork.setup: you're the new king of Egypt. a foreign people in your land has grown large. you don't remember why they came. what do you do?
options: honor them for what their ancestor did for Egypt.
call them a threat and put them to forced labor.
fork.reveal: he says they are more and mightier than we, sets taskmasters over them, and makes their lives bitter. it began with forgetting.

original.note: Hebrew: names. the Jewish title of the book, from its opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: Exodus is about the plagues and the sea.
what it means: it begins with a ruler who forgot, fear of neighbors, and lives made bitter by forced labor.

what a scholar hears: the store city Raamses shares its name with Pharaoh Ramesses II, so some link the story to his reign, but Exodus never names the king, and historians still debate its date and setting.
